871.quote_or_event: “Farid, the Creator is in the Creation, and the Creation abides in God. Whom can we call bad? There is none without Him.”
871.explanation: In a salok placed among Farid's, Guru Arjan reasons that since God dwells in every creature, there is no one we may write off as bad.
871.tie_back: The Kural says enmity has no good in it and should not be courted even in jest; Guru Arjan removes the ground for enmity altogether, since no one is without God.
871.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1381, Salok Sheikh Farid (salok 75, Mahalla 5), Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
871._accuracy_note: Reasonable fit: both reject enmity outright, but Gurbani's reason is theological (God in all), while the Kural judges enmity by its lack of any good quality.

872.quote_or_event: “Slandering the Saints, one’s life is cut short.”
872.explanation: In Sukhmani Sahib Guru Arjan warns that turning against the holy by slandering them shortens one's very life.
872.tie_back: The Kural warns never to make enemies of the wise whose plough is the word; Guru Arjan likewise warns that turning against the saints, people of the Word, brings ruin on oneself.
872.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 279, Raag Gauree, Sukhmani Sahib, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
872._accuracy_note: Strong thematic fit on the danger of opposing people of the Word; the Kural means scholars and counsellors generally, the Sukhmani means the holy, and the harm is spiritual rather than political.

873.quote_or_event: “O egotism, you are the root of birth and death and the cycle of reincarnation; you are the very soul of sin. You forsake friends, and hold tight to enemies.”
873.explanation: Guru Arjan addresses ahankar, pride, as the root of sin that makes a person drop friends and cling to enemies.
873.tie_back: The Kural calls the man who stands alone yet makes many enemies more foolish than a madman; Guru Arjan names the ego as the folly that drives friends away and gathers enemies.
873.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1358, Salok Sahaskriti (salok 49), Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
873._accuracy_note: Reasonable fit on losing friends and gathering enemies through pride; Gurbani names haumai/ahankar as the cause, while the Kural judges the strategic folly of standing alone.

874.quote_or_event: According to the Janamsakhi tradition retold by Macauliffe, robbers (thags) on the road surrounded Guru Nanak meaning to rob him; he gave them spiritual instruction, and they gave up their trade, began to repeat the Name, and reformed their lives.
874.explanation: Instead of fleeing or fighting, Guru Nanak turned men who came as his attackers into followers of the Name.
874.tie_back: The Kural praises the noble person who turns enemies into friends; in this story Guru Nanak does exactly that with men who came to rob him.
874.source: Max Arthur Macauliffe, The Sikh Religion, vol. 1 (1909), Life of Guru Nanak, ch. V, pp. 71-72 (paraphrase)
874._accuracy_note: Good thematic fit on winning over would-be enemies, but the episode is Janamsakhi hagiography retold by Macauliffe, not documented history.

875.quote_or_event: Britannica records that the Mughal emperor Jahangir, who had imprisoned Guru Hargobind in Gwalior fort, finally released him, apparently seeking the Sikhs' favour as possible allies against the Indian states still defying Mughal rule.
875.explanation: Facing several opponents at once, the emperor chose to turn one adversary, the Sikhs, into a potential ally rather than keep fighting on every front.
875.tie_back: The Kural advises one who faces two enemies alone to make one of them an ally; Jahangir's release of Guru Hargobind is an instance of that same calculation.
875._accuracy_note: Next-best: the strategy fits, but it is the Mughal emperor's calculation, not a Sikh teaching, and Britannica presents the motive as only apparent.

876.quote_or_event: “One who is not affected by pleasure or pain, who looks upon friend and enemy alike - says Nanak, listen, mind: know that such a person is liberated.”
876.explanation: Guru Tegh Bahadur describes the liberated person as one whose mind does not swing between friend and enemy.
876.tie_back: The Kural advises keeping a careful middle distance in a crisis, neither committing to nor breaking with a person; Gurbani also holds friend and enemy in the same even regard, though for a different reason.
876.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1427, Salok Mahalla 9 (salok 15), Guru Tegh Bahadur (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
876._accuracy_note: Next-best: the shared idea is evenness toward friend and foe, but Gurbani means spiritual detachment, while the Kural means cautious diplomacy in a crisis.

877.quote_or_event: “Tell your troubles to the One who is the Source of all comfort.”
877.explanation: Guru Nanak teaches that one's sorrows should be laid before God, the giver of all comfort, rather than spread before others.
877.tie_back: The Kural says not to tell your troubles to those who do not already know them, nor show weakness before enemies; Guru Nanak likewise directs the telling of troubles to God alone.
877.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 16, Sri Raag, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
877._accuracy_note: Reasonable fit on the first half (whom to tell one's troubles to); the reason is devotional, and the Kural's warning about showing weakness to enemies is not addressed.

878.quote_or_event: After the execution of Guru Arjan, Guru Hargobind trained in arms, built up a Sikh army and fortified his cities, built the Akal Takht at Amritsar in 1609 and the fort of Lohgarh, and later defeated Shah Jahan's forces four times.
878.explanation: Under pressure from Mughal power, the sixth Guru made his community strong and well defended, and is believed to have borne two swords at his succession for temporal (miri) and spiritual (piri) authority.
878.tie_back: The Kural says to know the right method, build up your strength and guard yourself, and the enemy's arrogance will fade; Guru Hargobind's build-up of Sikh strength and defences shows that strategy at work.
878._accuracy_note: Strong historical fit on building strength and defences against a proud enemy; the Guru framed it as defence of the faith (miri-piri), not as a general maxim of statecraft.

879.quote_or_event: “Fareed, the farmer plants acacia trees, and wishes for grapes.”
879.explanation: Farid uses the image of a farmer who sows thorny acacia yet hopes to harvest grapes, to show that what one lets take root decides what one later reaps.
879.tie_back: The Kural uses a thorn tree to teach that enmity must be cut while young before it hardens; Farid's thorny acacia makes the related point that what is allowed to grow determines the harvest.
879.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1379, Salok Sheikh Farid (salok 23), Bhagat Farid (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
879._accuracy_note: Next-best: shares the thorn-tree imagery and the logic of consequences, but Farid speaks of one's own deeds and their fruit, not of uprooting an enemy early.

880.quote_or_event: “They alone are truly alive, whose minds are filled with the Lord. O Nanak, no one else is truly alive; those who merely live shall depart in dishonor; everything they eat is impure.”
880.explanation: In a salok of Majh ki Vaar Guru Nanak says that only those filled with God are truly alive, and that those who merely live will leave the world without honour.
880.tie_back: The Kural says those who cannot break the pride of hostile enemies are not alive even to breathe; Guru Nanak shares the claim that mere breathing is not life and links life to honour, but places true life in the remembrance of God.
880.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 142, Raag Maajh, Majh ki Vaar (salok, Guru Nanak) (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
880._accuracy_note: Next-best: the structure (mere existence is not life; honour matters) matches, but Gurbani grounds true life in the Naam, not in defeating enemies' pride.
